newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Branson rivals expect balloon take-off on Monday.
newsitem.headline: Branson rivals expect balloon take-off on Monday.

text.p: A Belgian-Swiss team of balloonists said on Wednesday it aimed to set off for a round-the-world trip early next week and was unlikely to suffer the same problem that brought down Richard Branson's balloon.
"We're in the red zone. Probably (we will try to take off) on Monday night," Belgian Wim Verstraeten told VTM television.
Verstraeten and his Swiss partner Bertrand Piccard have been preparing for their trip with the Breitlinger-Orbiter balloon for the past three months in the Swiss town of Chateau D'Oeux.

They have become front-runners in the race to be the first to fly round the world by balloon after British tycoon Branson's attempt ended earlier on Wednesday, less than 24 hours after it began, because of technical problems.
"We're working in the same way (as Branson) but on top of our balloon we attached a tent to keep the valves free of ice," Verstraeten said.
He said Branson's mishap was not linked to weather conditions. "It's just a coincidence, stupid bad luck. It could be that everything went wrong because of a 50-franc ($1.5) sensor," he said.
He said that a piece of the tiny layer of ice which covered the top of Branson's balloon at night may have dropped into the gas valve controlling the release of helium.

"They probably tried to open the valve electronically and a piece of ice probably got in, preventing (the valve) from closing perfectly, so the balloon started descending and lost a lot of helium," he said.
"They could no longer control the descent and had to release the tanks to be able to land safely."
Verstraeten, who told Belgian newspapers he had wished Branson the best of luck before the take-off, admitted he was relieved, but not because the Briton's attempt had failed.
"I'm relieved in the sense that no one is injured. It would have been a blow to our morale if someone had been seriously injured or killed," he said.
Verstraeten said Branson would have served as a "guinea pig" for the Belgian-Swiss team which had to fly over countries like China and Russia.
"We would have liked to see what his strategy would have been," he said.
Verstraeten also said Branson's balloon, which like the Breitlinger was "experimental, the Formula One of ballooning", had lifted off too fast on Tuesday.
"He wanted to rise at three metres (10 ft) per second but we think he went at six metres (20 ft) per seconds....much too fast," Verstraeten said.
Officials of Branson's Virgin empire have cast doubt on whether the tycoon would have enough time for a second attempt this year.
American balloonist Steve Fosset also has plans for a round-the-world attempt, launched from St. Louis, Missouri.
